# Judge Q&A — prepared answers

*Generated by `presentation/build.py` from `artifacts/*.json`. All numbers come from classical simulation. No quantum hardware was used.*

## Is this novel?
The method is not. The ZZ feature map is from Havlíček et al. (2019). Bandwidth scaling of quantum kernels is from Shaydulin & Wild (2022), exponential concentration from Thanasilp et al. (2022), the geometric difference from Huang et al. (2021), and the corrected resampled t-test from Nadeau & Bengio (2003). What we contribute is a careful reality check that puts these pieces together in one reproducible open tool: a fold-safe, nested-CV benchmark against tuned classical models on the same features and splits, a bandwidth and concentration study, and a noise and circuit-count study, all on the same real data.

## What exactly did you find?
With its bandwidth tuned by nested CV, the quantum kernel beats the RBF SVM in 0 of 12 dataset × qubit settings (mean differences −1.9 pts to −0.4 pts; 12 of 12 95% CIs include zero). At the tutorial scaling s = 1, breast-cancer accuracy falls from 89.5% at 2 qubits to 66.0% at 12 (wine 88.3% → 66.9%). Best model per dataset: breast cancer: RBF SVM on 10 PCA features (97.7%) and RBF SVM on all 30 original features (97.7%), tied within 0.1 pts; wine: RBF SVM on 12 PCA features (99.8%).

## Where does the classical model win?
Everywhere on the RBF comparison: the tuned quantum kernel's mean is below the RBF SVM in all 12 of 12 settings. No single gap is significant on its own (12 of 12 CIs include zero; smallest p = 0.207), so the honest wording is "tied within noise, never ahead". The top model on each dataset is classical: breast cancer: RBF SVM on 10 PCA features (97.7%) and RBF SVM on all 30 original features (97.7%), tied within 0.1 pts; wine: RBF SVM on 12 PCA features (99.8%).

## Did the quantum kernel beat anything?
Nominally significant (p < 0.05) differences against logistic regression: wine at 2 qubits (+3.2 pts, CI [+0.1, +6.3], p = 0.045). That is 1 of 12 uncorrected tests, so it is weak evidence; with any multiplicity correction it disappears. Logistic regression is linear, so a nonlinear kernel beating it on a low-dimensional projection is expected and is not a quantum effect: the RBF SVM beats logistic regression there too (97.6% vs 93.6%).

## Why these datasets?
The Track 2 brief asks for a real dataset and small data. Wisconsin breast cancer (569 × 30) is the dataset most quantum-kernel tutorials use, so our result speaks to a common claim directly. Wine (178 × 13, cultivar 1 vs rest) is a second, smaller, imbalanced task (33.1% positive) that checks the pattern isn't specific to one dataset.

## How do you guarantee fairness?
- Identical outer splits for every model: 3x repeated stratified 5-fold (outer), stratified 3-fold (inner).
- Identical features: StandardScaler → PCA(n) → MinMax [0, π], fitted on each training fold only. `tests/test_core.py::test_preprocessing_is_fit_on_training_fold_only` changes the test fold by ×100 and checks the training features don't move.
- Identical tuning budget: every hyperparameter (C ∈ [0.1, 1.0, 10.0, 100.0], RBF γ ∈ [0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1.0, 3.0], bandwidth s ∈ [0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 1.0]) is chosen by the same inner stratified 3-fold CV on the training fold; the test fold is used once.
- Paired comparison on the same folds, with the Nadeau–Bengio correction (variance × (1/J + n_test/n_train)), because overlapping training sets make the naive t-test overconfident. A unit test checks the corrected CI is wider than the naive one.

## What is the bandwidth s and why does it matter?
The features are multiplied by s before encoding. At s = 1 (the usual tutorial setting) the encoded states of different samples are nearly orthogonal at larger qubit counts, so the kernel matrix approaches the identity and the SVM memorises. Smaller s keeps states close, which restores a useful similarity structure (Shaydulin & Wild 2022). Our inner CV chose s ≤ 0.1 in 158 of 180 outer folds (median 0.05) and s = 1 in 0.

At s = 1 the variance falls about 2.7× per qubit from 2 to 14 qubits. It is below ~1/1,000 (the resolution of 1,000 shots) from 8 qubits and below ~1/100,000 from 12. Treat 1/shots as a rough floor: the exact estimator variance is k(1 − k)/shots.

## What is the geometric difference and what does it tell you?
g(K_C‖K_Q) (Huang et al. 2021) measures how much better the quantum kernel could generalise than a classical kernel K_C on this data, in the worst case over labels. g ≈ 1 means the classical kernel can already express anything the quantum kernel can. With both kernels trace-normalised and a 10⁻³ ridge, at the small bandwidths CV actually picks, g = 1.2–3.1 against the best RBF kernel. The largest value in our scan, g = 28.1, is at s = 1 and 2 qubits, a setting whose quantum kernel scores 89.5% against 94.4% for the RBF SVM. Large g is necessary for an advantage, not sufficient: the quantum kernel also has to suit the labels. At s = 1, g falls again at high qubit counts because both kernels approach the identity.

## How hardware-aware is this?
- Each kernel entry is a compute-uncompute overlap circuit (feature map for x, inverse feature map for y, measure P(0…0)). A test checks this probability equals our statevector kernel.
- Noise study: breast cancer, 40 train / 30 test, 1,980 circuits per qubit count, 1,000 shots, bandwidth = the median CV choice. `AerSimulator.from_backend(FakeTorino())`: FakeTorino (historical snapshot bundled with qiskit-ibm-runtime; run locally in Aer). Transpiled with optimization_level=1 and a fixed seed. No error mitigation.

| qubits | s | CZ | depth | RMSE, 1,000 shots | RMSE, FakeTorino | mean off-diag k exact / noisy | accuracy exact / shots / noisy |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 0.05 | 22 | 102 | 0.010 | 0.266 | 0.862 / 0.599 | 80.0% / 86.7% / 76.7% |
| 6 | 0.05 | 38 | 142 | 0.012 | 0.307 | 0.787 / 0.479 | 96.7% / 93.3% / 86.7% |

Accuracy here uses the best C on the 30-sample test set, so it is optimistic, and one sample is 3.3 points. Read the RMSE columns, not the accuracies.

Transpiled cost of one overlap circuit on FakeTorino:

| qubits | CZ | depth |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 4 | 30 |
| 4 | 22 | 102 |
| 6 | 38 | 142 |
| 8 | 54 | 182 |
| 10 | 70 | 222 |
| 12 | 86 | 262 |

Full breast-cancer dataset, one CV fold: 103,285 train pairs + 51,870 test pairs = 155,155 circuits. Our full protocol (7 bandwidths × 15 outer folds, one qubit count) would need ≈ 11,622,975 circuits, about 12 billion shots at 1,000 shots each. An RBF kernel for the same fold takes milliseconds.

## Would real hardware change the conclusion?
It could only make the quantum kernel worse here: the exact (noise-free) kernel already doesn't beat the RBF SVM, and the noise model distorts entries ~25× more than shot noise. Error mitigation could reduce the distortion, but not past the exact kernel's accuracy. We did not run on hardware and used no IBM account.

## What would it take for a quantum kernel to win?
Data whose structure matches the feature map (Huang et al. 2021 construct such datasets), a kernel with large geometric difference to every classical kernel *and* good alignment with the labels, and a bandwidth that avoids concentration. Our bench measures all three, so it can be pointed at a new feature map or dataset to test such a claim.

## How do you know the code is right?
`tests/test_core.py` checks: batched NumPy statevectors equal Qiskit's `zz_feature_map` statevectors (2, 3, 4, 6 qubits); the kernel is symmetric, PSD, unit-diagonal and in [0, 1]; the overlap circuit's P(0…0) equals the kernel; preprocessing is fitted on training folds only; g of identical kernels is 1; the Nadeau–Bengio CI is wider than the naive one.

## Multiple comparisons?
We report 24 paired tests against the RBF SVM and logistic regression, uncorrected. Correction would only remove the single nominal quantum win; every "classical wins or ties" statement holds without it.

## What is reusable for the community?
`qkbench` is a small MIT-licensed package: a fast tested fidelity kernel, a fold-safe nested-CV benchmark with corrected tests, concentration and geometric-difference diagnostics, and a shot/noise harness for overlap circuits. Swapping in another dataset or feature map is a few lines, and the deck, abstract and these answers regenerate from the saved JSON.
